$comment: Policy enforced by runtime/acp-policy-proxy/index.mjs on every ACP
session/request_permission. This is the real enforcement point for this
workspace - see knowledge/enforcement-model.md for why .cursor/cli.json and
session mode `ask` are NOT sufficient on their own.
Evaluation order, fail-closed:
1. Any deniedPattern matching the raw command  -> DENY
2. Any segment whose command base is not in allowedCommands -> DENY
3. git with a subcommand not in git.allowedSubcommands -> DENY
4. Tool kinds outside allowedToolKinds -> DENY
5. Anything not explicitly permitted -> DENY
Compound commands are split on && || ; and | and every segment is checked,
so `git log && aws s3 ls` is denied on the second segment.

git.$comment: branch/tag are omitted deliberately: `git branch -D` and `git tag -d` are destructive, and subcommand-flag parsing is not worth the risk here.

sensitivePatternsComment: Applied to the title AND the resolved paths of EVERY tool kind, not just execute. repos/nkb_backend/env_prod.sh carries the prod DB password, Django SECRET_KEY, MSG91/OneSignal/SES credentials and an Algolia admin key, so a plain read of it is as damaging as any command.

$comment: Injected into the agent-acp child environment by the shim, replacing any
ambient AWS variables. Critical: on this machine AWS_PROFILE=default is a
DIFFERENT ACCOUNT (nxtwave-tech) than the one this POC is scoped to
(nxtwave-alpha). Inheriting it would point the agent at production while
every config file claimed otherwise.
Credentials live in runtime/aws/credentials (gitignored, mode 600). On ECS
that file is absent and the task role is used instead, with no change here.

network.$comment: A web search or fetch is an egress channel: anything the agent has read can be embedded in the query string. The audit log already shows it searching for internal identifiers unprompted. Off until there is a reason to turn it on.

$comment: MCP admission is ToolHive's, not this file's.
allowedServers and awsApi used to live here: a per-server tool allowlist,
and a parser that read the AWS CLI command out of call_aws arguments and
checked the service and operation against a list. Both are gone.
What replaced them, with the evidence rather than the intention:
- tool admission -> ToolHive. Excluded tools are refused on tools/call,
not merely hidden from tools/list. See
evaluations/migration-baseline/toolhive-admission.json and
rapid7-admission.json.
- AWS operation authorization -> IAM. ecs delete-service and
iam create-user return AccessDenied through the governed path. See
evaluations/migration-baseline/aws-boundary.json.
- the Rapid7 allowlist -> config/toolhive/servers.yaml, where it is
derived from upstream readOnlyHint annotations rather than hand-listed.
sqlQuery stays. Section 32 ties its removal to DBHub plus a real read-only
database role proving the engine refuses writes, and neither exists yet.
It is the one place in this file still deciding a security outcome from a
string, and it should be the next thing deleted.
Statement-level gating for database tools. The authoritative controls are
a SELECT-only database user and an Aurora reader endpoint, which rejects
writes at the engine regardless of grants. This layer sits above both: it
refuses a destructive or exfiltrating statement before it reaches the
network and names it in the audit log.
Comments are stripped before the keyword is read, and multi-statement
requests are refused, because both hide intent behind a benign first word.
sql-probe is a stub that touches no database; it exists so this gating can
be exercised without one. See knowledge/rds-access.md for why no real
server is attached yet.

audit.$debugPayloads: Writes untruncated permission payloads alongside the audit log. Used once to establish that Cursor does send tool arguments, which is what makes per-operation gating of call_aws possible; see mcp.awsApi. Off by default because payloads carry full arguments -- turn it on only to work out the shape of a new tool.
